hook: You know a sign hung over Jesus on the cross. But did you know the four Gospels give its words four different ways, and agree on the charge?
story:
Each of the four Gospels stops at the same moment. The soldiers have done their work, and a sign hangs above Jesus’ head. Then each writer tells us what it said.

Mark: “THE KING OF THE JEWS.” Matthew: “THIS IS JESUS, THE KING OF THE JEWS.” Luke: “THIS IS THE KING OF THE JEWS.” John: “JESUS OF NAZARETH, THE KING OF THE JEWS.”

Four Gospels, four wordings. Even the name for the sign changes. Mark calls it “The superscription of his accusation”, Matthew “the accusation against him”, Luke “An inscription”, and John “a title”, which Pilate wrote himself.

Look closely at what differs. Matthew opens with “THIS IS JESUS,” John with “JESUS OF NAZARETH,” Luke with only “THIS IS”, and Mark gives the bare charge. Now look at what does not differ. All four have the same words, “THE KING OF THE JEWS.” None of them says the sign read anything else.

Then John gives a detail that changes the question: “it was written in Hebrew, in Latin, and in Greek.” In the World English Bible Luke says it too, that the inscription stood there “in letters of Greek, Latin, and Hebrew”, though several printed Greek editions leave these words out of Luke. One sign, three languages. And John explains why so many saw it: “many of the Jews read this title, for the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city”.

moment:
The charge on the sign is the charge of the whole trial. In all four Gospels Pilate’s first question to Jesus is the same: “Are you the King of the Jews?” In John, Jesus answers, “My Kingdom is not of this world.”

The soldiers turned the title into mockery. They put a robe and a crown of thorns on him, knelt, and saluted him, “Hail, King of the Jews!” In John the accusers pressed Pilate with the same word: “Everyone who makes himself a king speaks against Caesar!” And when Pilate asked, “Shall I crucify your King?”, the chief priests answered, “We have no king but Caesar!”

So the sign over the cross was no slogan made up on the spot. It was the charge that ran through the whole trial, written out as the reason for the sentence. John says Pilate wrote it himself, and the chief priests came straight back with an objection: “Don’t write, ‘The King of the Jews,’” but write that he only claimed it. Pilate’s answer is short: “What I have written, I have written.”
around:
Matthew sets the sign in a crowd of voices. The soldiers sit down and watch. Two robbers hang on either side. People passing by shake their heads, and the chief priests mock: “If he is the King of Israel, let him come down from the cross now, and we will believe in him.” In Luke the soldiers throw the words of the sign at him: “If you are the King of the Jews, save yourself!” He does not come down.

Matthew had used this title long before the trial. At the start of his Gospel, wise men from the east arrive in Jerusalem asking, “Where is he who is born King of the Jews?” In Matthew the title is spoken soon after his birth and written over his death, both times by people who were not Jews.
after:
The charge did not stay on the cross. Years later, in Thessalonica, a crowd dragged Jesus’ followers before the city rulers with an accusation that sounds like the sign again: “These all act contrary to the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus!”

The sign itself became a relic. Around the year 383 a pilgrim named Egeria described a silver-gilt casket brought out in Jerusalem, and the wood of the cross and the title laid on a table. In Rome, the church of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme keeps a walnut board with lines in Greek and Latin letters, which tradition links to Helena, the mother of Emperor Constantine. It was found hidden behind a brick in 1492. Three radiocarbon tests have dated the wood between 980 and 1146, and most scholars treat it as medieval, though a few still defend it.

The words lasted longer than any board. By the tenth century crucifixes in the West carried the Latin initials INRI, for Iesus Nazarenus Rex Iudaeorum, and Eastern icons carry the Greek letters INBI. Pilate wrote the words as a charge. Churches still set them above the cross.
readings:
Readers have explained the four wordings in several ways.

One answer points to the three languages. A sign written in Hebrew, Latin and Greek need not have said exactly the same thing in each, and the Bible commentator Albert Barnes suggested that each Gospel writer may have rendered a different line.

A second answer says John gives the fullest form, and the others kept the part that mattered most, the charge itself. Eric Lyons of Apologetics Press compares it to three people quoting the same billboard, each giving more or less of the wording.

A third answer looks at how ancient writers reported words. Simon Greenleaf, a professor of law at Harvard, held that the Gospel writers give the sense rather than the exact wording, and Michael Licona lists paraphrase among the methods that ancient biographers used.

A fourth note is about copying. In John the three languages stand in every printed Greek edition that Bible Hub shows. In Luke several editions, such as Westcott and Hort’s of 1881 and Tischendorf’s, leave them out, while the Byzantine text keeps them, as the World English Bible does.

And skeptics answer that the four simply disagree about what the sign said, which is the claim Lyons sets out to answer. Each of these readings starts from the same fact: on the charge itself, all four agree.
point: Set side by side, the four Gospels do not give the same words for the sign over the cross. They give the same charge. The difference is real, and so is the agreement, and the agreement is the heart of the sign, the part all four kept: he was crucified as “THE KING OF THE JEWS.”
lesson:
When four people tell you what a sign said, you do not expect four identical sentences. You listen for what all of them say. Read the four accounts of the sign that way, and they say one thing together: Jesus died under the name of king.

That leaves you with a question older than any list of contradictions. Pilate asked it, the soldiers mocked it, the chief priests tried to edit it, and Pilate would not change it: is he a king? The sign gave Pilate’s answer. The Gospels leave the answer to you.

If you want to weigh it, read the trial in John 18 and 19 in one sitting and notice how often the word king comes back. And if you do not share this faith, there is still something here worth noticing: about the sign, the one thing all four writers agree on is the charge that killed him.

echoes.note: Paul reminds Timothy of Christ Jesus “who before Pontius Pilate testified the good confession”. The man under the sign had not denied the charge.
The sign spoke three languages. John’s vision sees a crowd “out of every nation and of all tribes, peoples, and languages” standing before the Lamb.
Pilate wrote one title over the cross. Revelation shows another name written on the garment of the rider: “KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS.”
Days before the cross, Jesus rode into Jerusalem on a donkey, as this prophecy says: “Behold, your King comes to you!” The king was announced before he was charged.
